A browser asks for a resource, and a server answers with a status, headers and content. Follow a page request from the first name lookup to the HTML that arrives at your screen.

DNS supplied an address. TCP established an ordered connection, then HTTP carried a request and the HTML response. The browser can now parse the document and fetch its other resources. Replay to follow the journey again.
The browser separates the host name from the path in the address. Before it can send HTTP, it needs an IP address and an established TCP connection.
The client asks its resolver for the IPv4 address of www.example.com. A reply associates that name with 203.0.113.10 so the browser can address its connection.
A SYN begins the connection and proposes sequence numbers. The server acknowledges it with SYN-ACK, and the client sends the final ACK. Both endpoints now track the byte stream.
The browser sends a GET request for the root document. The server replies with 200 OK and HTML. TCP divides the response into segments and delivers their contents in order.
The browser parses the returned HTML into a document tree. It lays out the elements and paints the page. References to images or stylesheets would trigger more requests.
The next device on this local link. Remote traffic is sent to the router.
Identifies the protocol inside the frame.
IPv4 with a fixed header and no options.

Helps reassemble fragmented datagrams; this value is illustrative.

Each router subtracts one. Zero prevents endless circulation.

HTTPS places HTTP inside an authenticated encrypted connection. The browser still resolves a name and opens TCP, but TLS protects the request and response from observers along the path.

DNS found the address and TCP opened the stream. TLS authenticated the server and established traffic keys before HTTP sent the page request. The browser received and decrypted the response locally, leaving observers with encrypted records rather than the page contents.
The https scheme asks the browser to use TLS before sending HTTP. The host name also identifies the service whose certificate must be checked.
A name still needs an address
The client resolves www.example.com to an IPv4 address. Encryption of the later HTTP exchange does not by itself encrypt a conventional UDP DNS lookup.
A three-way handshake establishes TCP state at both endpoints. Port 443 selects the HTTPS service, while the client uses an ephemeral port.
Agree on keys and verify the server

The client offers a TLS version, cipher suites and a key share. The server selects compatible parameters and proves its identity through a certificate and signature. Both sides confirm the handshake before ordinary application data.
The browser’s GET request is encrypted before it enters TCP. The server encrypts the response too. A packet observer can see endpoints and record sizes, but cannot read the HTTP content.
TLS authenticates and decrypts received records locally. The browser then interprets the HTTP response and renders the HTML, just as it would after an unencrypted HTTP transfer.
Compatibility value, not the negotiated protocol version.
Length of the following handshake message.
Begins negotiation or selects the server’s parameters.
An illustrative handshake nonce; real values differ.
No legacy session ID in this minimal example.
The offered or selected authenticated-encryption suite.
Supported versions and key shares negotiate the connection.
Compatibility signal; it does not select TLS 1.3 keys.
TLS 1.3 also hides handshake and alert content inside this outer type.
The negotiated version is carried in the hello extensions.
Includes protected content, an inner content type and authentication tag.
A teaching placeholder, not recoverable plaintext or real cryptographic output.
TCP gives applications an ordered byte stream. Sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission let it recover from loss without asking the application to assemble packets itself.
A byte stream survives packet loss

The receiver buffered later data while a missing range held back delivery. Duplicate acknowledgments and a SACK block identified that hole. Retransmitting the missing 100 bytes let the receiver acknowledge the complete 300-byte stream before both sides closed.
The client sends SYN and the server responds with SYN-ACK. A final ACK completes the handshake. Each side now knows the other side’s initial sequence position.
The first segment carries bytes 1 through 100. The receiver acknowledges 101, meaning it now expects that byte next.
One segment is lost on the path

The sender transmits two more ranges of the stream. The middle range is lost, while the later range reaches the receiver. TCP can buffer that later data without presenting an incomplete stream to the application.

The receiver keeps acknowledging 101 because that byte has not arrived. A selective acknowledgment reports the later range it already has. The sender can distinguish the missing data from buffered data.
The sender retransmits the missing range. Once it arrives, the receiver can advance its cumulative acknowledgment past all three ranges and release the contiguous stream.
A FIN says the sender has no more stream data. Both directions are acknowledged and closed independently. The endpoints then release their connection state after the appropriate closing period.
UDP sends individual messages without a transport handshake. It preserves datagram boundaries but leaves recovery, ordering and timing decisions to the application.
The application owns the timing policy

Voice frames left without a transport handshake. One datagram was lost, but subsequent frames continued on schedule. RTP supplied ordering and timing information, while the application chose how to handle the missing audio.
The first voice frame can leave immediately. UDP adds source and destination ports, a length and a checksum, without establishing a TCP-style connection.
A new voice frame every 20 ms
The sender encodes small pieces of audio into separate datagrams. RTP sequence numbers and timestamps describe their order and playback timing. UDP itself does not interpret those media fields.
One datagram fails to reach the receiver. UDP has no automatic retransmission, so the next voice frame continues on schedule. The receiver notices the gap through the RTP sequence number.
The remote endpoint sends voice frames back to the client’s port. These are independent messages rather than TCP acknowledgments. The application manages the two media streams.
Balance late data against missing data

A voice application may conceal the missing sound rather than wait for a late retransmission. A different UDP application could implement its own reliable delivery. UDP leaves that policy above the transport layer.
RTP is carried inside each UDP datagram.
The application negotiates this payload mapping separately.
Lets the receiver detect missing or reordered voice frames.
IP addresses packets and forwards them between networks. Routers select the next hop using the destination address; the link-layer envelope changes at each hop while IP spans the route.

ARP found the gateway’s local MAC address, and an Ethernet frame carried a remotely addressed IP datagram to that gateway. Routers forwarded it toward the destination while reducing TTL. The capture remained on the home network, before outbound NAT and after reverse translation of the reply.
Compare destination with the local subnet

The client compares its subnet with the destination address. 203.0.113.10 is outside 192.168.1.0/24, so the default route points to 192.168.1.1. The server’s IP stays the destination even though the first link goes to the router.
The laptop broadcasts an ARP request for the gateway’s local address. The router answers with its MAC address. ARP does not discover the remote web server’s MAC across the Internet.
A local frame holds a remote datagram

The Ethernet destination is the router, while the IPv4 destination is the web server. The laptop sends the encapsulated packet on the local link. The router removes that link envelope before forwarding it.
Routing and address translation are distinct

A typical home router translates the client’s private source address and records a mapping. Every router along the route also decrements TTL and chooses a next hop. This capture is taken before NAT, so it retains the client’s private address.
The response follows routes toward the translated address. The home router uses its mapping to deliver it to 192.168.1.10. The local capture shows that packet after reverse translation.
Broadcast to every device on the local link.
The network address family to resolve.
MAC addresses are 6 bytes; IPv4 addresses are 4.
A request asks who owns the target IP.
Unknown in the request; supplied in the reply.
DNS connects readable names with resource records. A recursive resolver can follow the naming hierarchy, cache what it learns and return a result to the client.
Delegation leads to an authoritative answer

The recursive resolver followed the root, top-level domain and authoritative server to obtain the requested address. It returned that answer to the client and cached it for the record’s lifetime. A later lookup can reuse valid cached data instead of repeating every exchange.

The laptop asks its recursive resolver for www.example.com. If no usable cached answer exists, the resolver continues on the client’s behalf. The client does not normally contact each authority itself.
Start at the top of the hierarchy

The resolver asks a root server where to continue. The root points toward the top-level domain’s name servers rather than returning the final web address. Referrals reduce the problem one delegation at a time.
The resolver contacts a .com server next. That server identifies the authority for the example domain. The resolver can cache delegation information as well as final answers.
Ask the server responsible for the zone
The authoritative server holds the domain’s published records. It returns an A record associating www.example.com with 203.0.113.10. This completes the resolver’s search for the requested address.
Reuse the result until its TTL expires

The resolver returns the address to the laptop and caches it for its remaining TTL. Later queries can avoid the full hierarchy while the record remains valid. A DNS TTL is a cache lifetime, separate from the hop-limiting IPv4 TTL.
DHCP supplies an address lease and the network settings a host needs. A client discovers a server, selects an offer and receives confirmation before using the configuration.

Discover, Offer, Request and Acknowledge established the client’s lease. The configuration included a router and DNS resolver as well as an address. A later unicast renewal extended the lease without repeating the initial broadcast discovery.
A new client knows its link-layer identity but lacks usable IPv4 settings. It cannot yet use the normal default gateway or resolver. DHCP bootstraps that configuration on the local network.
The client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER so a local server can hear it. UDP ports 68 and 67 identify client and server. A transaction ID lets everyone recognize replies to this negotiation.
The server offers 192.168.1.10 for a limited lifetime. Options describe the subnet, gateway and DNS resolver. An offer is a proposal, not yet the client’s final authorization to use the address.

The client requests the offered address and identifies the chosen server. Broadcasting this selection also tells other DHCP servers that their offers were not selected. The address is still subject to the server’s confirmation.
DHCPACK confirms the lease and repeats the settings. After checking that the address is safe to use, the client configures its interface. It can now contact the gateway and resolve names.
Keep the lease before it expires

At the renewal time, the configured client normally unicasts DHCPREQUEST to its server. An ACK extends the lease. If renewal fails for long enough, the client must eventually stop using the expired address.
DHCP reuses the BOOTP message structure.
Identifies the client hardware address format.
Groups all messages in this address negotiation.
An unconfigured client may require broadcast replies.
Zero until the client has a usable address.
The address offered or acknowledged by the server.
No boot server or relay in this example.
The client identifier on the local Ethernet.
Legacy server-name and boot-file fields are unused.
Marks the beginning of DHCP options.
TLV options communicate message type and network configuration.
ICMP reports network conditions and supports diagnostic probes. Ping measures replies, while traceroute uses expiring hop limits to reveal responding routers along a path.

An echo exchange tested the destination and supplied a round-trip measurement. Probes with increasing TTL illustrated how traceroute discovers responding hops. A port-unreachable reply showed that a packet can reach a host even when no application accepts its destination port.
Ask the destination to echo data

The client sends an ICMP Echo Request to the server. An identifier and sequence number distinguish the probe. A reply can demonstrate reachability, though a missing reply alone does not prove the host is down.
Match the reply to the request

The destination returns an Echo Reply containing the original echo data. The sender matches its identifier and sequence number, then measures elapsed time. This is a round-trip measurement rather than one-way latency.
A traceroute probe starts with TTL 1. The home router decrements it to zero and discards the packet. An ICMP Time Exceeded message quotes the beginning of that original datagram.
The next probe has a larger TTL and can travel farther. The next responding hop sends its own Time Exceeded message. Real paths may have nonresponding hops or change between probes.
Build a path from repeated probes
Increasing TTL step by step reveals a sequence of responding hops. Each response measures a separate round trip from the client. It does not guarantee that every packet takes an identical path.
Report that a service cannot receive

A UDP probe can reach the destination but find no application listening on its port. The host may answer with ICMP Destination Unreachable, code 3. Traditional UDP traceroute uses that reply as its destination signal.
Gives a more specific reason within the message type.
Matches probes to the program that sent them.
Matches a reply to its individual probe.
The receiver copies these bytes into its reply.
Identifies the packet that caused this error.
SMTP submits and relays messages using a command-and-reply conversation. A sending server looks up the recipient domain’s mail exchanger, then transfers responsibility to another server.
Submission and relay have different roles

The client submitted mail over a protected connection, and the sending server looked up a mail exchanger. Server-to-server SMTP used a separate connection and upgraded it with STARTTLS. The final acceptance transferred delivery responsibility; it did not reveal whether the recipient had read the message.
EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA
The client opens TCP port 465 and negotiates TLS immediately. Only after that protection is ready does SMTP begin. This submission connection is distinct from server-to-server relay.

The server advertises its SMTP capabilities after EHLO. The user authenticates over the protected connection before submitting mail. The packet view shows encrypted records, while the lesson explains their role.

MAIL FROM and RCPT TO specify the transport envelope. DATA then carries the message headers and body, ending with a dot on its own line. A success reply means this server has accepted responsibility for the message.
Look up the destination mail exchanger
The sending server asks DNS for MX records of the recipient domain. MX preference numbers help order the candidate mail servers. The relay then resolves and connects to the selected exchanger.
Upgrade a relay connection with STARTTLS
Mail servers normally relay using port 25. When STARTTLS is available and selected, the connection upgrades to TLS before the mail transfer continues. A new EHLO follows the TLS handshake.
The receiving server accepts the message

The recipient’s server accepts the relayed message and places it in a mailbox or delivery queue. SMTP acceptance is not evidence that a person has read it. Retrieval protocols handle the later mailbox access.
POP3 provides a compact conversation for listing and retrieving messages. It suits download-oriented clients, with deletion applied only after the session successfully enters its update phase.
Retrieval followed by an explicit update

The client authenticated, listed the mailbox and retrieved a complete message. DELE marked that message, and a successful QUIT committed the deletion. Omitting DELE would have let the client retain the server copy.
USER, PASS, STAT, RETR, DELE, QUIT
TCP connects to the POP3 service on port 995. TLS is negotiated before credentials or mail commands. The server’s identity must be verified before the client trusts that connection.

The server greets the client and accepts authentication commands inside TLS. A successful response moves the session into the transaction state. Example credentials explain the flow without representing a real account.
STAT returns the message count and total size. LIST can provide individual message numbers and sizes. These numbers identify messages within this POP3 session.
RETR asks for a message by its session number. The server returns its headers and body as a multiline response. Dot-stuffing distinguishes data lines from the terminating dot.
Commit marked deletions on clean exit
DELE marks a message for deletion during this session. QUIT enters the update phase and commits those marks when successful. A client may instead keep server copies by choosing not to send DELE.
IMAP manages mail stored on the server. Clients select mailboxes, fetch selected content and synchronize flags, allowing multiple devices to work with the same mailbox state.
Fetching does not remove the message

The client selected INBOX and fetched content by UID while leaving the message on the server. IDLE then allowed the server to announce a mailbox change. This separation of server storage, content retrieval and state updates supports synchronized clients.
The client connects to port 993 and establishes TLS before speaking IMAP. Protection applies to credentials, mailbox metadata and content. The server then sends its protocol greeting.
Use tags to match completion replies
A tagged command authenticates the user inside TLS. The server repeats that tag in its completion response. Tags let a client associate responses with commands even when unsolicited updates arrive.
Select a mailbox and learn its state
SELECT opens INBOX for message operations. The server reports message count, flags and UID validity information. Stable UIDs are more useful for synchronization than sequence numbers that may shift.

The client fetches a message or a selected part of it. BODY.PEEK avoids setting the Seen flag merely by retrieving the data. The message remains on the server unless an explicit removal workflow is used.
The client enters IDLE to receive mailbox changes without repeated polling. A server update can announce a new message. DONE ends IDLE so the client can issue further commands.
FTP separates its command conversation from file data. A control connection coordinates authentication and transfer setup, while a second connection carries the selected file.
Control and content take separate connections

FTP kept its commands on port 21 and negotiated a passive data port for the file. The data stream closed when the transfer ended, while the control stream reported success and handled QUIT. Both streams were visible in this plain FTP example.
Keep commands on one TCP stream
The client opens TCP port 21 for FTP control messages. The server’s 220 greeting indicates that it is ready for a session. This connection will coordinate the later data transfer.
An unprotected FTP login is visible
USER and PASS authenticate the session. In this plain FTP example, both commands are readable on the wire. A protected protocol is needed when credentials must be confidential.
Ask the server for a data listener

PASV asks the server to listen on a separate port. Its reply encodes an address and two port octets. The client initiates the data connection, which usually works more easily through a client-side firewall.
A second TCP stream carries the file

The client connects to the advertised data port and requests a file on the control connection. The server can now deliver file bytes independently of its status replies. The two TCP streams have different endpoint ports.
Transfer bytes, then close the data stream

File contents arrive on the data connection. Closing that stream signals the end of this transfer, and a control reply confirms success. Another file may use a new data connection while the control session stays open.
QUIT ends the FTP session after transfers are complete. The server responds before closing the control connection. Neither of the two plain FTP streams provides encryption by itself.
SSH authenticates a remote host and protects interactive sessions. Its transport negotiates algorithms and keys before user authentication and logical channels are carried inside encrypted packets.
Host identity, user identity, then channels

SSH exchanged banners, negotiated algorithms and authenticated the host during key exchange. The client then proved its user identity without sending its private key. Session channels carried encrypted input and output inside the established transport.
TCP connects to port 22, then both peers exchange SSH version banners. These identification lines are initially readable. They help the peers choose a compatible SSH transport.

Each peer sends KEXINIT with supported key-exchange, host-key and encryption algorithms. Compatible choices are selected from these lists. Negotiating an algorithm is separate from authenticating the host’s identity.
Establish keys and verify the host

Ephemeral public keys support agreement on shared secret material. The server signs the exchange with its host key, which the client checks against a trusted identity. NEWKEYS switches subsequent packets to the negotiated protection.
Prove possession without sending a private key
The client requests user authentication over the protected transport. A signature proves control of an authorized private key. The private key itself stays on the client.

The client opens a session channel inside the SSH connection. It may request a terminal and an interactive shell. Channel identifiers and flow-control windows let several activities share the protected transport.

Input travels as channel data and the remote process returns its output on that channel. Observers see encrypted packets rather than the command text. Closing the channel need not immediately close every other activity on the SSH connection.
At least four random padding bytes align the transport packet.
The unencrypted key-exchange payload; values are illustrative.
Illustrative padding; every real exchange uses fresh randomness.
Packet length, payload and authentication tag depend on the negotiated cipher. These bytes are illustrative.

TLS protects application data with authenticated encryption. A handshake negotiates parameters, authenticates the server and derives traffic keys; subsequent records hide their content from the network.

The hellos selected TLS 1.3 parameters and exchanged ephemeral public keys. Certificate verification and Finished messages bound the connection to an identity and the handshake transcript. Authenticated encryption then protected application records until the closing alerts.
Application data and later handshake messages
Offer parameters and an ephemeral key

The client offers supported TLS versions, cipher suites and a public key share. A server-name extension identifies the requested virtual host in this example. The ClientHello is visible here because encrypted client hello is not being used.
Select parameters and derive handshake keys
The server selects TLS 1.3 and a mutually supported cipher suite. Its key share lets both sides derive handshake protection keys. Messages after ServerHello are generally encrypted in TLS 1.3.
Bind the server to a verified identity

The encrypted handshake includes the certificate chain and a proof using its private key. The client checks the chain, host name and applicable validity rules. A certificate is useful only when those checks connect it to a trusted identity.

Finished authenticates the accumulated handshake messages using derived key material. Both endpoints verify this confirmation. A transcript mismatch prevents the connection from being treated as successfully established.

Application data is sealed into TLS records with authenticated encryption. An authentication tag lets the receiver reject altered data. The packet inspector marks protected content as unknown instead of inventing plaintext bytes.
Signal the end of protected data
A close_notify alert indicates that an endpoint has finished sending TLS records. In TLS 1.3 it is protected like other post-handshake content. TCP then handles the underlying stream shutdown.
